summary: Kitaoka and Ashida report a new anomalous motion illusion, named the "central drift illusion," in which observers see illusory motion in a stationary image without any retinal slip, and it can be seen in both central and peripheral vision. The illusion appears in visual phantoms, Zavagno's figures, ring-of-ellipse and rounded-head shapes, and striped squares, and the critical factor seems to be contrast (direction described as low-to-high or high-to-low contrast). The note also records demonstrations shown at the VSJ 2004 winter meeting, related illusions, and an intention to propose a model and submit a manuscript.
one_line: Kitaoka and Ashida present the "central drift illusion," a stationary-image motion illusion seen in central and peripheral vision without retinal slip, driven by contrast.
key_facts: Akiyoshi Kitaoka (Ritsumeikan University) and Hiroshi Ashida (Kyoto University) presented the central drift illusion at the 2004 winter meeting of the Vision Society of Japan, Tokyo, January 26-28, 2004.
The central drift illusion is a new anomalous motion illusion in which observers see illusory motion in a stationary image without any retinal slip.

The peripheral drift illusion, described in Kitaoka and Ashida, 2003, VISION, was previously the only anomalous motion illusion known to not require retinal slips, and it cannot be seen in central vision.
The central drift illusion can be seen in both central vision and peripheral vision.
The critical factor for the central drift illusion seems to be the difference in contrast between the inner and outer areas of elongated bars or ellipses.
Pseudo second-order phantoms strongly induce the illusory motion, in which phantoms bridging low-contrast stripes appear to expand in the horizontal direction.
When the contrast of Zavagno's figure decreases, the anomalous motion illusion increases.
When the ellipses in the ring figure are rotated through 90 degrees, the rings appear to rotate slowly.
The illusion does not depend on the luminance gradient of inducers; the direction of illusory motion is set by contrast, described as "low-to-high" contrast in one subtype.

The other subtype, with squares of horizontal stripes that appear to expand horizontally, is described as "high-to-low" contrast and is characterized by luminance edges rather than luminance gradients.
The demonstration of the high-to-low subtype was not supported by many people at the VSJ meeting.
The central drift illusion seems to start with some delay after the change of gaze.
The central drift illusion is strong when the luminance gradient is drawn along the longer axis of inducers, while the peripheral drift illusion is strong when the gradient is along the shorter axis.
Apparent positional shifts are induced by the central drift illusion, with upper and lower vertically aligned ellipses appearing shifted.
The authors propose to call the new illusion the "central drift illusion" and say they will soon propose a model explaining its mechanism and submit a manuscript to an academic journal.
